reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ESC & ACC-AHA guidelines
clinicalPearls: WPW describes ventricular pre-excitation from an accessory pathway together with symptomatic tachyarrhythmia; the resting ECG classically shows a short PR interval, a delta wave, and a widened QRS
The most common arrhythmia is orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia, a regular narrow-complex tachycardia using the AV node antegrade and the accessory pathway retrograde

The dangerous arrhythmia is atrial fibrillation conducted rapidly down the accessory pathway, producing an irregular, broad, bizarre, and very fast ventricular response that can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation
In pre-excited atrial fibrillation, AV nodal blocking drugs are contraindicated because they can accelerate conduction over the accessory pathway
An unstable patient with a pre-excited tachyarrhythmia should undergo urgent synchronised cardioversion
The term WPW pattern refers to asymptomatic pre-excitation on ECG, whereas WPW syndrome requires accompanying arrhythmia
Catheter ablation of the accessory pathway is highly effective and is often curative, and is preferred in symptomatic patients
Risk stratification assesses how rapidly the pathway can conduct, since a short refractory period predicts higher risk during atrial fibrillation
reference.pathophysiology: In WPW an accessory atrioventricular pathway bypasses the normal AV nodal delay, allowing early activation of ventricular myocardium and producing the delta wave and short PR interval. This creates the substrate for reentry: in orthodromic AVRT the impulse travels down the AV node and back up the accessory pathway, while in the less common antidromic form the direction is reversed, giving a wide-complex tachycardia. The gravest scenario occurs when atrial fibrillation develops and the accessory pathway, lacking the rate-limiting properties of the AV node, conducts rapid atrial impulses to the ventricles, risking degeneration to ventricular fibrillation and sudden death.
additionalDifferentials: AV nodal reentrant tachycardia without an accessory pathway
Atrial fibrillation or flutter with aberrant conduction
Other causes of a short PR interval
Bundle branch block mimicking a broad QRS
additionalInvestigations: 12-lead ECG to identify pre-excitation and characterise arrhythmia
Ambulatory monitoring to capture paroxysmal tachyarrhythmias
Exercise testing to assess for abrupt loss of pre-excitation as a marker of a longer pathway refractory period
Electrophysiology study to localise the pathway and measure its conduction properties
Echocardiography to assess for associated structural disease such as Ebstein anomaly
redFlags: MEDICAL EMERGENCY: pre-excited atrial fibrillation with a rapid, irregular, broad-complex response that can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation
Haemodynamic instability during any pre-excited tachyarrhythmia requiring urgent synchronised cardioversion
Syncope or aborted sudden cardiac death indicating a high-risk pathway
Use of AV nodal blocking agents in pre-excited atrial fibrillation, which can precipitate deterioration
reference.prognosis: Most patients have an excellent prognosis, and catheter ablation is curative in the great majority; the principal risk is sudden death from rapidly conducted atrial fibrillation in the minority with a short-refractory-period pathway, which risk stratification and ablation substantially reduce.
pitfalls: Administering AV nodal blocking drugs in pre-excited atrial fibrillation
Assuming an asymptomatic WPW pattern requires no assessment when risk stratification may be warranted
Mistaking pre-excited atrial fibrillation for ventricular tachycardia or ordinary atrial fibrillation
Delaying cardioversion in an unstable pre-excited tachyarrhythmia
management: Catheter ablation of the accessory pathway is the definitive, curative treatment and is offered to symptomatic patients
Acute orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia terminated with vagal manoeuvres followed by AV-nodal blockade such as adenosine
In pre-excited atrial fibrillation, AV-nodal blocking drugs are avoided and rhythm controlled with procainamide or flecainide, or urgent cardioversion
Immediate synchronised DC cardioversion for any haemodynamically unstable pre-excited tachyarrhythmia
Risk stratification of asymptomatic pre-excitation using exercise testing for abrupt loss of pre-excitation and, where indicated, an electrophysiology study
Antiarrhythmic drugs such as flecainide or propafenone as an alternative when ablation is deferred or declined
Cardiology and electrophysiology referral, with echocardiography to screen for associated Ebstein anomaly
